The key result is that the plateau's output directions contain almost no channel 163 (0.7% of their energy), while layer 9's post-attention norm gain on channel 163 is 450 against a median of about 20. So the "94% on channel 163" write is indirect. The plateau adds a near-constant diffuse vector that inflates the RMS of layer 9's attention output, and the RMSNorm then shrinks the bulk's own channel-163 contribution, which the gain of 450 multiplies.

The plateau therefore acts as an RMS damper on layer 9's attention, the same for every kind of text. That matches what we saw: removing it does not reliably help math (pooled DEV about +0.2 points) and causes looping. I consider the L9 line closed.

The re-read notes also remind me that head ablations in this architecture are confounded by this same post-attention RMS rescaling. The spectral scan only catches low-rank plants. A planted change could also be per-unit: a neuron or head scaled down or up, or zeroed. That leaves no low-rank trace, but it would show up as an outlier in per-unit weight norms, or as exact zeros.

So I'll do a weight-only scan of every layer:
- MLP neurons: robust z-scores of the gate-row, up-row and down-column norms;
- attention: per-head norms of the q/o blocks and the k/v norms;
- exact-zero counts in every matrix.

A planted unit should stand out as an extreme outlier (|z| > 8, or exact zeros) in one or a few layers; a smooth picture closes the per-unit line.

The scan finds no exact zeros, and no attention head is an outlier. Every k/v projection has Frobenius norm ≈ 16, which suggests near-unit rows: uniform and apparently a property of training. The MLPs show something to follow up in the late layers (12–17), in two parts:
- **Heavy gate tail:** many neurons have very large gate-row norms (z up to 45).
- **Up/down low outliers:** some neurons combine a normal or huge gate with tiny up and down weights (z ≈ −7 to −10). Examples are L13 n204 (gate z = +27, up −7.4, down −9.3), L14 n575 and L16 n378.

A neuron that still gates strongly but whose output path (up × down) was shrunk is exactly what a hand-planted attenuation of capability neurons would look like. Natural dead neurons usually shrink in all three matrices together.

To tell these apart, I'll list, per layer, every neuron with a low up or down norm (z < −5) together with its gate z, and the shape of the gate-norm distribution:
- **Planted:** a cluster of such neurons concentrated in some layers, whose gate rows stay normal or large.
- **Natural:** a few scattered neurons that are small in all three matrices, or a smooth heavy tail.

The low-output list is long (401 neurons, cut off) and smooth rather than clustered. In the late layers (12–17), dozens of neurons per layer combine a large gate with up/down norms at about half the median. The minimum up and down ratios are only 0.31–0.55 of the median in every layer, so there is no ×0.1-style planted attenuation.

This is the natural sharp-gate pattern. GeGLU lets a large gate norm trade off against smaller up and down weights, which gives the same output with a sharper gate. Together with the earlier spectral scan, this closes the per-unit attenuation line in the projection matrices: no zeros, no outlier heads, no isolated scaled-down neurons.

One place a planted change would be invisible to all of these scans is the RMSNorm gain vectors. A few channels' gains changed in one layer is a diagonal edit with no low-rank or per-unit trace. That is also exactly the lever behind the channel-163 effect I just found.

I'll do a weights-only scan of the four norm types across the 18 layers. Each layer's gain vector is normalised by its median, and each channel is then compared with that channel's median across layers. I'll list the most extreme isolated deviations and count negative effective gains.
- **Planted:** a handful of channels with large deviations confined to one layer.
- **Natural:** smooth variation, or the same massive channels being large in every layer.

The norm-gain scan finds a pattern that none of the earlier scans could see: several effective gains are exactly 0.0, meaning stored weights of exactly −1.0. They appear where the same channel has large gains in the other layers.

The most striking case is layer 4's post-feedforward norm. It has 18 strongly deviating channels, including five (436, 232, 188, 547, 360) whose effective gain is exactly 0, against cross-layer medians of 30–55. That means layer 4's MLP output is completely cut off on those channels. Others are isolated: post-attention L2 ch133, L3 ch149, L0 ch542, L9 ch218, and post-feedforward L1 ch93. The pre-feedforward zeros on channel 400 in layers 0–5 look like systematic massive-channel handling, which is natural.

A gain landing exactly on 0 is implausible as a training outcome but trivial as a hand edit ("silence these channels"), so this could be a planted suppression. It could also be a learned way to keep MLPs from writing into outlier channels.

To decide, I'll check:
- which gains are bit-exactly −1.0, per norm and layer, against near-zero but inexact ones;
- the full list of layer 4's deviating post-feedforward channels, with their gains in layers 3 and 5 and how much layer 4's MLP down-projection writes into them.
- **Natural:** zeros only on massive or outlier channels where the MLP's down weights are also negligible.
- **Planted silencing:** exact zeros on ordinary channels that layer 4's MLP writes strongly.
